ci-one-proportion-s1.title: Skipping breakfast at a large university
ci-one-proportion-s1.text: A dietitian at a university with 28,000 students selects a random sample of 400 students. Of them, 248 say they regularly skip breakfast. She wants to estimate the proportion of all students at the university who regularly skip breakfast.

ci-one-proportion-s2.title: One poll, three intervals
ci-one-proportion-s2.text: A city council selects a random sample of 600 residents, and 324 of them ($\hat{p} = 0.54$) favor longer library hours. A computer builds three confidence intervals for the proportion of all residents who favor longer hours, at 90%, 95% and 99% confidence, and lists them in random order.

table.caption: Three intervals from the same sample, levels not shown

items.q: Which statement correctly checks the large counts condition for a confidence interval?
options: 248 skip and 152 do not, and both are at least 10
$n = 400$ is at least 30
400 is less than 10% of 28,000

why.correct: For an interval, $p$ is unknown, so check the observed successes and failures: $n\hat{p} = 248$ and $n(1 - \hat{p}) = 152$, both at least 10.
options: Right: for an interval, check the sample's successes and failures.
The rule of 30 is about means. For a proportion, check successes and failures.
That is the 10% condition, which is about independence, not the normal shape.
No value of 0.5 is claimed here. For an interval, use the sample's counts, 248 and 152.

items.q: Calculate the standard error of $\hat{p}$. Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is $\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}$ before the square root. Take the square root to get the standard error.
That is $\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}$ with no division by $n$. Divide by 400 inside the square root.
That uses 0.5 in place of $\hat{p}$. An interval's standard error uses the sample proportion, 0.62.

why.correct: $\hat{p} = \frac{248}{400} = 0.62$ and $\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.62(0.38)}{400}} = 0.0243$. It uses $\hat{p}$ because $p$ is unknown.

items.q: Calculate the margin of error for a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all students who regularly skip breakfast. Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That uses $z^* = 1.645$, the critical value for 90% confidence. For 95%, $z^* = 1.96$.
That uses $z^* = 2.576$, the critical value for 99% confidence. For 95%, $z^* = 1.96$.
That is the standard error alone. Multiply it by the critical value, 1.96.

items.q: Construct a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all students at the university who regularly skip breakfast.

why.correct: $0.62 \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.62(0.38)}{400}} = 0.62 \pm 0.048$, which gives the interval from 0.572 to 0.668. Technology (a one-proportion z interval) gives the same.

items.q: Type the 95% confidence interval as an expression with the values substituted: the point estimate, then +/-, then the margin of error.

mistakes.why: The standard error needs a square root: $\sqrt{0.62(0.38)/400}$.
1.645 is the critical value for 90% confidence. For 95%, use 1.96.
Divide by $n$ inside the square root: $\sqrt{0.62(0.38)/400}$, not $\sqrt{0.62(0.38)}/400$.

items.q: Which interval was built with 99% confidence?
options: Interval 1
Interval 2
Interval 3
There is no way to tell, because they come from the same sample

why.correct: Higher confidence needs a larger critical value (2.576 for 99%), so the margin of error is largest. Interval 2 reaches farthest from 0.54 on each side (from 0.488 to 0.592).
options: Interval 1, from 0.500 to 0.580, is in the middle: it is the 95% interval.
Right: the largest margin of error comes from the largest critical value.
Interval 3 has the smallest margin of error, so it has the lowest confidence, 90%.
Same sample, same $\hat{p}$ and standard error, but different critical values, so different margins of error.

items.q: What is the margin of error of Interval 1?

why.correct: The margin of error is half the distance between the ends: $\frac{0.580 - 0.500}{2} = 0.040$. Equivalently, it is the distance from $\hat{p} = 0.54$ to either end.
options: Right: half the distance between the two ends.
That is the whole distance from one end to the other. The margin of error is half of it.
That is the center of the interval, the point estimate, not the margin of error.
That is the standard error. The margin of error is the standard error times $z^* = 1.96$.

items.q: Suppose the council had surveyed 2,400 residents and still found $\hat{p} = 0.54$. About what would the margin of error of the 95% interval be?

why.correct: The margin of error is $z^*\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}$. With 4 times the sample size it is divided by $\sqrt{4} = 2$: about $\frac{0.040}{2} = 0.020$.
options: Right: 4 times the sample size halves the margin of error.
The sample size is inside a square root, so 4 times the residents divides the margin by 2, not 4.
A larger sample gives a smaller margin of error; it does not stay the same.
More residents give a more precise estimate, so the margin of error shrinks.

items.q: For a new poll, the council wants a 95% margin of error of at most 0.02. Using 0.54 as its estimate of the proportion, what is the smallest sample size it needs?

why.correct: Solve $1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.54(0.46)}{n}} \le 0.02$: $n \ge \left(\frac{1.96}{0.02}\right)^2(0.54)(0.46) = 2385.5$. Round up to 2,386 residents (always round a sample size up).
options: The calculation gives 2,385.5, and a sample size is always rounded up, or the margin would be a bit over 0.02.
That uses 0.5 in place of 0.54. It is the safe choice when there is no estimate, but this question says to use 0.54.
That uses $z^* = 1.645$, the critical value for 90% confidence. For 95%, use 1.96.

items.q: Find the critical value $z^*$ for a 90% confidence interval. Give three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That puts 90% below $z^*$, leaving all 10% in one tail. Split the 10% into two tails of 5%: area 0.95 below $z^*$.
1.96 is the critical value for 95% confidence. For 90%, it is 1.645.

why.correct: A 90% interval leaves 5% in each tail, so $z^*$ has 95% of the standard normal area below it: $z^* = 1.645$.

items.q: Find the critical value $z^*$ for a 98% confidence interval. Give three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That puts 98% below $z^*$. A 98% interval leaves 1% in each tail, so the area below $z^*$ is 0.99.
2.576 is the critical value for 99% confidence. For 98%, it is 2.326.

why.correct: 98% in the middle leaves 1% in each tail, so $z^*$ has 0.99 of the area below it: $z^* = 2.326$.

items.q: A wildlife officer wants to estimate the proportion of all deer in a state forest that carry a certain tick, from a random sample of 150 deer. Which procedure fits?
options: A one-sample z interval for a proportion
A one-sample z interval for a mean
A z interval that compares two groups of deer
A z-score for the 150 deer

why.correct: One population, one categorical variable (carries the tick or not), and the goal is an estimate: a one-sample z interval for a proportion.
options: Right: one sample, a proportion, an estimate.
Carrying a tick is a yes-or-no variable, so the parameter is a proportion, not a mean.
There is one group of deer, not two groups to compare.
A z-score locates one value in a distribution; it does not estimate a population proportion.

items.q: Why does the standard error for a confidence interval use $\hat{p}$ instead of $p$?
options: Because $\hat{p}$ is closer to 0.5 than $p$
Because using $\hat{p}$ makes the margin of error smaller
Because $p$ is unknown, so the sample value stands in for it
Because $\hat{p}$ is the parameter and $p$ is the statistic

why.correct: The formula $\sqrt{p(1 - p)/n}$ needs $p$, which is what we are trying to estimate. We substitute the sample's $\hat{p}$, and the result is called the standard error.
options: There is no reason $\hat{p}$ would be closer to 0.5; it is used because it is what we have.
The substitution is made because $p$ is unknown, not to shrink the margin.
Right: the standard error estimates $\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ from the data.
It is the other way round: $p$ is the parameter, $\hat{p}$ the statistic.

items.q: A student takes a random sample of 40 skateboards from a skate park and finds 4 with cracked decks. Why should she not build a one-sample z interval for the proportion of all the park's skateboards with cracked decks?
options: Because 40 is less than 30
Because there are only 4 successes, fewer than 10
Because 40 skateboards is more than 10% of the population
Because a proportion of 0.10 is too small to estimate

why.correct: Large counts requires at least 10 successes and 10 failures in the sample. There are only 4 cracked decks, so the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ may be skewed and the normal critical value would not give the stated confidence.
options: For proportions the check is successes and failures, not the sample size; and 40 is more than 30 anyway.
Right: large counts fails, so the normal model is not justified.
Nothing says the park has fewer than 400 skateboards, and the 10% condition is not the main problem here.
Small proportions can be estimated; the problem is that the sample has too few successes.

items.q: A pollster builds a 95% confidence interval for a proportion from a random sample. Which changes would make the margin of error smaller? Select all that apply.
options: Taking a larger random sample
Using 99% confidence instead of 95%
Using 0.5 in place of $\hat{p}$ in the standard error
Sampling from a population 10 times as large, with the same sample size

why.correct: The margin of error is $z^*\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}$. Only a larger $n$ shrinks it here. Raising the confidence level raises $z^*$; replacing $\hat{p}$ by 0.5 makes $\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})$ as large as it can be; and the size of a large population does not enter.
options: Right: $n$ is in the denominator of the standard error.
Higher confidence needs $z^* = 2.576$, a larger margin of error.
$0.5(0.5) = 0.25$ is the largest possible value of $\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})$, so the margin of error cannot shrink this way.
Population size does not appear in the formula when the sample is under 10% of it.

items.q: The dietitian's 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all students at her university who regularly skip breakfast runs from 0.572 to 0.668. Build the interpretation of this interval.

options: We are 95% confident that
There is a 95% probability that
95% of students say that

why.1: Once built, the interval either captures the true proportion or not; the 95% describes the method, so say "confident".
why.2: The 95% is not a percent of students; it is the confidence level of the method.

options: the interval from 0.572 to 0.668 captures
the sample proportion falls between 0.572 and 0.668
95% of the data fall between 0.572 and 0.668

why.1: The sample proportion is 0.62 for certain; the interval is about the unknown population value.
why.2: An interval for a proportion says nothing about where 95% of the data fall.

options: the true proportion of all students at the university who regularly skip breakfast
the proportion of the 400 sampled students who skip breakfast
the proportion of days a typical student skips breakfast

why.1: The sample proportion is known (0.62); the interval estimates the population proportion.
why.2: The variable is whether a student regularly skips breakfast, not how many days.

conclude.model: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.572 to 0.668 captures the true proportion of all students at the university who regularly skip breakfast.

why.correct: The interpretation names the confidence level, the interval, and the parameter in context: the proportion of all students at the university, not the 400 in the sample.
